title: The Rock Ampersand Roll Hall of Fame
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame: their personal feelings about museums and memorabilia, Johnny Rotten's rejection of induction, the founding by Ahmet Ertegun of Atlantic Records and the push for a hall of fame, the Cleveland versus New York and other city vote (Cleveland won with about 110,000 more votes than Memphis), Cleveland's fundraising, the 1995 first induction class, the building by architect I.M. Pei, the 1995 opening concert, the induction process and its criticism (voters, 25-year rule, sexism, genre gaps), award categories (Ahmet Ertegun Award, Early Influence, Musical Excellence), induction ceremony speeches and reunion drama (Blondie, Axl Rose, Mike Love), notable snubs (Chic, Judas Priest, Iron Maiden, Jane's Addiction, Dick Dale), hip hop inclusion debate with Ice Cube and Gene Simmons, the museum's exhibits and the Garage, George Harrison's posthumous induction jam, and failed New York and Tokyo outposts. Ends with a listener email.

entities.name: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame

segments.title: Opening banter and museum fandom
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with Simpsons banter, then discuss their feelings about rock memorabilia in museums. Chuck has not been to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and is not keen to go; Josh likes seeing real artifacts, such as Prince's jumpsuit and Mick Jagger's leather pants, and Seattle's pop culture museum.
topics: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame visit

segments.title: Rock museum paradox and Johnny Rotten's rejection
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the paradox of putting rock and roll behind glass in a museum. Johnny Rotten of the Sex Pistols wrote a refusal calling the Hall a pisstain and urine in wine. Josh argues the museum still embodies rock spirit and that museum display is simply what museums do.

segments.title: Origins: Ahmet Ertegun, Atlantic Records and Cleveland's rock roots
segments.summary: Ahmet Ertegun, co-founder of Atlantic Records, first proposed a rock hall of fame in New York. Atlantic signed R&B acts then rock acts. Businessmen in Cleveland were already planning their own hall. Cleveland's rock credentials include DJ Alan Freed, who is credited with coining rock and roll, WJW radio, and the 1952 Moondog Coronation Ball. Several famous musicians came from Cleveland or Akron.

segments.title: City vote, Cleveland fundraising, and first induction class
segments.summary: The Foundation opened a vote among Cleveland, Memphis, New Orleans, Philadelphia, San Francisco and New York. Cleveland won the USA Today poll by about 110,000 votes, with Memphis second, and raised $26 million. The first induction class was held in New York, including Chuck Berry, James Brown, Ray Charles, Sam Cooke, Elvis, Little Richard and others. A 1995 critic called the honor the most civilized.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the building discussion.

segments.title: Admission and the building designed by I.M. Pei
segments.summary: Admission is about thirty dollars, and temporary exhibits make repeat visits possible. Architect I.M. Pei designed the building, which has a glass pyramid evoking a guitar neck, a central tower, and a circular plaza shaped like a turntable. The building cost about a hundred million dollars, and the hosts discuss the Seinfeld architect joke.

segments.title: Groundbreaking concert and induction criteria
segments.summary: The Hall opened with a multi-hour concert at Cleveland Muni Stadium featuring Chuck Berry, Springsteen, Johnny Cash, Aretha Franklin, Al Green and Lou Reed. Induction requires being at least 25 years past the debut album and demonstrating musical excellence, criteria that critics call vague and subjective.

segments.title: Voting process, fan vote and sexism critique
segments.summary: Staff compile nominees, around a thousand musicians and industry members vote, and inductees need at least five percent of the vote. The hosts discuss the fan vote, which adds a single vote, the criticism that only about eight percent of inductees are women, and Dee Snyder's campaign for Iron Maiden.

segments.title: Award categories and multiple inductions
segments.summary: The Ahmet Ertegun Award, Early Influence Award and Musical Excellence Award are described. Tina Turner, Carole King, Stevie Nicks, Eric Clapton and The Beatles were each inducted more than once.

segments.title: Ceremony speeches, reunion drama and Axl Rose
segments.summary: The hosts recall awkward or emotional ceremony moments: Blondie's Debbie Harry refusing to let former members play, Paul McCartney's absence from the Beatles induction, Mike Love's combative speech, and Axl Rose's statement that he should not be inducted in absentia.

segments.title: Snubs and hip hop inclusion debate
segments.summary: Snubs discussed include Alice in Chains, Big Star, Dick Dale, the Smiths, MC5, Jane's Addiction, Motorhead, Judas Priest, Chic and Weird Al. Hip hop inclusion is debated with Ice Cube's remarks that rock and roll is a spirit and Gene Simmons's rebuttal. The hosts also note the 2021 class, including Tupac and Jay-Z, and Todd Rundgren and the Foo Fighters.

segments.title: Exhibits, the Garage and George Harrison jam
segments.summary: The museum has instruments, costumes, handwritten lyrics and master tapes, plus The Garage, a hands-on music room. The hosts recall George Harrison's posthumous induction jam, when Jeff Lynne and Tom Petty backed him on While My Guitar Gently Weeps. The New York and Tokyo outposts both closed, supporting Cleveland as the right choice.

segments.title: Listener mail: Lauren from Denver
segments.summary: A listener writes that a Josh mix-up about Led Zeppelin's song Friends made her and her father laugh, and the two share Zeppelin tattoos.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Show closing and a request to email listener stories.
